oneSentence: Regularisation changes a model's training objective or procedure to reduce overfitting and improve performance beyond the training data.
plainExplanation:
When a model is trained, optimisation reduces a loss: a number that measures how wrong its predictions are on the training data. Regularisation changes the objective or another part of the training procedure to reduce overfitting.

What goes in is the usual training data, the model, and one or more regularisation settings. A weight is a number inside the model that affects its output. A common method adds a penalty to the loss when weights become large. Another regularisation method, dropout, switches off some units temporarily during training, but it is a different technique from weight decay.

With penalty-based regularisation, optimisation balances two aims: fit the data and avoid overly complex settings. The combined loss might be written as prediction loss plus a penalty term. If the penalty is too weak, the model may still fit noise. If it is too strong, the model can become too simple and miss real patterns.

What comes out is usually a model that performs a little less perfectly on the training set but better on new data. In other words, regularisation often trades some training accuracy for better generalisation. It does not guarantee improvement, and regularisation settings are hyperparameters that need testing.

everydayAnalogy.title: Adjusting an equaliser for more than one song
everydayAnalogy.story: Imagine adjusting every slider on an equaliser until one song sounds perfect. Extreme settings may correct tiny quirks in that recording but make the next song sound worse. Adding a cost for extreme slider positions encourages a more restrained setting. The first song may sound marginally less perfect, but a wider range of songs sounds better. Regularisation similarly discourages a model from making large or numerous adjustments merely to match its training examples.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: Real regularisation does not literally judge whether a pattern is suspicious or faulty. It changes a mathematical objective during training. Also, not all regularisation works by discouraging large weights: dropout, early stopping, and data augmentation act differently, so the 'cost on adjustments' story fits some methods better than others.

visual.title: Training without and with regularisation
visual.learningObjective: Show how adding a penalty changes the training objective and can improve performance on new data even if training fit becomes slightly worse.
visual.description: A side-by-side diagram compares two training paths. The left path minimises prediction loss alone. The right path minimises prediction loss plus a regularisation penalty. Read from top to bottom in each column, then compare the final models and their behaviour on training versus new data.

steps.label: Same starting point
steps.explanation: Both columns start with the same training data and the same model architecture.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw two equal columns labelled 'No regularisation' and 'With regularisation'. At the top of both, show the same dataset icon feeding into the same model icon.

steps.label: Different objective
steps.explanation: The left column uses prediction loss only. The right column uses prediction loss plus a penalty that discourages large or overly flexible parameter values.
steps.visualInstruction: In the left column, show a box labelled 'optimise prediction loss'. In the right column, show a box labelled 'optimise prediction loss + penalty'. Add a small side note: 'penalty strength = hyperparameter'.

steps.label: Parameter updates
steps.explanation: Optimisation updates the weights in both cases, but the regularised path pushes against very large weights.
steps.visualInstruction: Show arrows from each objective box to weight sliders. In the right column, add a counter-force arrow or spring icon opposing extreme slider positions.

steps.label: Result on training data
steps.explanation: The unregularised model often reaches lower training loss because it can fit more detail, including noise.
steps.visualInstruction: At the bottom left, show a training-loss badge reading 'very low'. At the bottom right, show a training-loss badge reading 'slightly higher'.

steps.label: Result on new data
steps.explanation: The regularised model often performs better on unseen examples because it relies less on accidental patterns in the training set.
steps.visualInstruction: Below both columns, add a test-data row. Show the left model with a 'less stable on new data' badge and the right model with a 'more stable on new data' badge.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping each column highlights the objective used and swaps a small caption between 'fits training data closely' and 'generalises better to new data'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram compares two training processes side by side. Both begin with the same dataset and the same model. On the left, training minimises prediction loss only. On the right, training minimises prediction loss plus a penalty that discourages extreme parameter values. The left path ends with very low training loss but weaker behaviour on new data. The right path ends with slightly higher training loss but better performance on unseen data. The main point is that regularisation changes the objective during training so the model is less likely to fit noise.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static two-column comparison replaces any highlighting. Each column shows the same starting dataset and model, a different objective box, then a final note: left column, lower training loss; right column, better generalisation on new data.

workedExample.scenario: A programme officer in a regional bureau is testing a classifier that assigns themes to cleared project summaries before the first reading of a progress report.
workedExample.input: The same classifier is trained twice on labelled summaries, with separate validation and test sets. One version has no penalty; the other uses L1 regularisation.
process: The first version minimises classification loss alone.
The second minimises classification loss plus λ||w||₁, which penalises the absolute size of its weights and can drive less useful weights to zero.
Several values of λ are compared on the validation set. The choice is based on performance beyond the training data, not on which version fits the training examples most closely.
The selected regularised model is then checked once on the unseen test set.
workedExample.result: The regularised classifier may fit the labelled summaries slightly less closely while assigning themes more reliably to new summaries. If the penalty is too strong, however, it will underfit, so λ still requires validation.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A reporting officer in a Headquarters department is testing a model to code open-ended answers from a needs assessment into themes before the monitoring report goes for clearance.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Without regularisation, the model may fit incidental wording in the earlier answers rather than patterns that transfer to new responses. Adding a penalty during training can reduce that overfitting, with the strength selected against held-out data.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Needs-assessment answers may contain personal or protection-sensitive details. Raw responses must not be entered into a tool that has not been approved for that material. Regularisation does not prevent memorisation, provide anonymisation or make an unsuitable service safe.

whyItMatters: If you only look at how well a model matches its training data, you can choose a system that looks excellent during training but performs poorly in real use. Regularisation matters because it helps teams prefer models that are more dependable on new cases, not just impressive on old ones. For non-specialists, this affects procurement, evaluation, risk, and trust: a slightly less perfect training score may be the safer operational choice if it means fewer surprises later.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Regularisation simply makes a model smaller.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Sometimes it leads to smaller weights, but the main point is to change training so the model avoids overly specific solutions. A model can keep the same architecture and still be regularised through penalties, dropout, or other methods.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If regularisation raises training loss, it must be making the model worse.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. Training loss measures fit to examples already seen. Regularisation often accepts a small rise there to improve performance on unseen data, which is usually the real goal.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Weight decay, L2 regularisation, and dropout are all identical.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are related but not identical. L2 regularisation adds a penalty on weight size to the objective. Weight decay is often used as a close synonym, though in some optimisers the exact update differs. Dropout instead randomly removes units or connections during training, so it works through a different mechanism.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Regularisation changes training to reduce overfitting. It may add a penalty or use another method so the model usually works better on new data.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Regularisation modifies the optimisation objective or training procedure to reduce overfitting and improve generalisation. In the common penalty-based form, the objective becomes empirical loss plus a term such as λ||w||² for L2 or λ||w||₁ for L1, where w are parameters and λ controls strength. This biases training toward solutions with smaller or sparser weights. In deep learning, 'weight decay' is often used as a near-synonym for L2 regularisation, but the equivalence depends on the optimiser implementation; for example, decoupled weight decay in Adam is not identical to simply adding an L2 penalty to the loss. Broader uses of the word regularisation also include methods such as dropout, early stopping, label smoothing, and data augmentation, which reduce overfitting through different mechanisms rather than the same penalty term.

keyTakeaway: Regularisation alters training to discourage overfitting. Its strength is tuned on held-out data, since too little may not help and too much can cause underfitting.

quickCheck.question: What is the main purpose of regularisation during model training?
options: To make training data larger without collecting new examples
To force the model to fit the training set as closely as possible
To reduce overfitting by discouraging overly complex parameter settings
To guarantee that the model will converge to the global minimum
quickCheck.explanation: Regularisation is mainly used to improve generalisation by reducing overfitting. Depending on the method, it may add a penalty, alter training examples, or change the training procedure. It does not guarantee a global minimum or require collecting more data.

contested: The broad idea is widely accepted, but terminology can vary. Some people use 'regularisation' narrowly for penalty terms such as L1 or L2, while others use it more broadly to include methods like dropout, early stopping, and data augmentation. 'Weight decay' is also often treated as equivalent to L2 regularisation, although in some optimiser implementations the update rule is not exactly the same.

issues.problem: This defines all regularisation as adding a penalty or constraint. The page later includes dropout, early stopping and data augmentation, which change the training procedure or data rather than necessarily adding a penalty or constraint. The definition contradicts the page's own technical explanation.
issues.fix: Regularisation changes a model's training objective or procedure to reduce overfitting and improve performance beyond the training data.

issues.problem: The opening says regularisation always changes the training goal, which is false for methods such as early stopping and data augmentation. It also says dropout removes connections. Standard dropout switches off units or activations; masking connections or weights describes a different mechanism.
issues.fix: State that regularisation can change the objective or another part of training. Describe dropout as temporarily switching off units, not removing connections.

issues.problem: The visual presents penalty-based regularisation as if it were the mechanism of regularisation in general. Every path uses a penalty and pushes against large weights, despite the page later classifying methods such as dropout and data augmentation as regularisation.
issues.fix: Retitle it "Training without and with an L2 penalty" and describe it throughout as one common form of regularisation rather than the general mechanism.
